newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin pays price for all-out campaign.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin pays price for all-out campaign.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, who announced on Thursday that he had to have a heart operation, threw his all into his successful campaign to win a second term in the Kremlin and now appears to be paying the price.
Few politicians in the world have faced so many battles, taken so many risks and handled problems of such a scale. It is little wonder that his heart is failing him.

Yeltsin, having risen as a Communist Party official, then became leader of the first legal opposition in the Soviet Union, crushed the party and went on to play a pivotal role in destroying the Soviet Union.

He then launched first market reforms in the former superpower and, in what might be considered his gravest mistake, sent Russian forces to crush independence-seeking Chechnya in a war which cost many thousands of lives.

He suffered two mild heart attacks last year and was out of action for several months. But he pulled out all the stops in his re-election campaign to prove that he was fit for four more years at the top.
He criss-crossed the vast Russian Federation, keeping to a punishing schedule and adding flourishes like swinging on a swing and dancing the twist at a pop concert.
Gone was the halting walk, the slurred speech and the puffy face which had stirred rumours that heavy drinking and a weak heart might be taking their toll on the 65-year-old leader.
But the campaigning Yeltsin, who ressembled the man who climbed on a tank in August 1991 to defy a communist-led putsch in Moscow, disappeared suddenly when his goal was in sight.

He cancelled a string of appearances in the week before the runoff vote on July 3, in which he finished 14 points ahead of communist Gennady Zyuganov, and he looked stiff and awkward in a final appeal to voters.

He has since remained largely out of sight, appearing only briefly for his inauguration on August 9 and in several short, heavily-edited television appearances where his speech was not slurred but he moved slowly and carefully.
Yeltsin, elected Russian president in 1991, hit the peak of his power, strength and popularity in August of that year when he defied a hardline coup against Mikhail Gorbachev, the last Soviet leader.

But, two years after personifying the fight for democracy on the tank outside the White House, his moral authority slipped when he sent in tanks against the same parliament building to put down a bloody rebellion by hardliners in parliament.
In late 1994 he committed what he later acknowledged was a huge blunder, sending troops into Chechnya.

He said after last year's two mild heart attacks that he would rather retire and play with his baby grandson than face the stress of a second term in the Kremlin. But the threat of a communist return to power kicked him out of such lethargy.

His renewed activity recalled the energy and ambition that enabled Yeltsin, a construction engineer by profession, to buck authority and defeat the odds since his days as a Communist Party official in the Urals industrial city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg.
When Gorbachev brought him to Moscow in 1985, he rose quickly to become a candidate member of the party politburo, then the highest power in the land, and first secretary of the party in the capital.
His demands for faster reform lost him favour and in late 1987 he was disgraced, told by Gorbachev he would never be allowed back into politics.
But in March 1989 he was elected to parliament in the country's first multi-candidate elections, gaining a phenomenal 89 per cent of the vote in Moscow.
In July 1990, he gambled again and stalked out of the Communist Party. While many liberals chose to stay in the party, Yeltsin's move brought him only increased popularity.
In June 1991 he won some 57 per cent of vote in the Russian Federation to become its first executive president.
Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin was born in a peasant family on February 1, 1931. He has a wife, Naina, two daughters and four grand-children.
